newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ results season prompts profit downgrades.
newsitem.headline: NZ results season prompts profit downgrades.

text.p: Flat-to-slightly-weaker corporate earnings have prompted brokers to generally lower their profit forecasts for the year, analysts said on Wednesday.
As the current reporting season nears its end, analysts have had little to cheer about, with most outcomes being either in line or below expectations.
Bankers Trust economist David Plank said it was clear from anecdotal evidence, plus company tax data, that profits were not growing.

"But the corporate sector has had a very good run, so you would expect it to go through periods when profit growth slows or goes negative, without there necessarily being doom and gloom," Plank said. "At this stage of the economic cycle it's about what you would expect to happen," he said.

Perhaps the most telling result for the market was from market leader Telecom Corp of New Zealand, which reported an eight percent decline in third quarter earnings to NZ$167.2 million, its first fall in four years.
Some brokers had begun downgrading Telecom as early as December last year, and more have followed suit since the February 18 result.
"Basically the outcome of this round of reporting has been for analysts to downgrade their forecasts in many cases," said Don Turkington, economist and principal at brokers Cavill White Securities.

The benchmark NZSE-40 Capital Index, on which Telecom carries the largest weighting with 25.02 percent, has suffered as the season has progressed. The index, which stood at 2,286.44 in late Wednesday trade, has fallen more than 150 points or six
percent since the start of the season.
"We've got a number of companies that are not showing any growth, and I suppose the prime one among those is Telecom," Turkington said.

Analysts are now looking at a flat result for Telecom for the year to March, and Cavill White expects a profit of NZ$717 million from $718 million a year ago, down from a previously forecast $770 million.
Corporate earnings had reflected a tough economic enviroment, particularly over the December quarter, with the retail sector being particularly hard hit.
"The problem we now confront is that, even despite the flat economy, we've still got pockets of inflation that make it unlikely the Reserve Bank will ease in the short term," Turkington said.
The Reserve Bank, which presents its six monthly economic projections on March 13, is not expected to ease monetary conditions, which have already tightened since late January.
There had been a glimmer of hope late last year that a decline in rates over 1997 would assist a recovery in earnings.
While the domestic economy has had its problems, they have paled against those in the forest sector, which makes up 22.49 percent of the NZSE-40.
A slump in pulp and paper prices has severely impacted on earnings and the outlook there, too, is uncertain.

Fletcher Paper reported a first half loss of NZ$40 million, reversing a NZ$186 million profit a earlier. FCL Forests and FCL Building also disappointed. Carter Holt Harvey came in with third quarter earnings of NZ$53 million, well short of forecasts.
On the other side of the commodities coin, FCL Energy performed strongly, rising to NZ$126 million from $20 million, due to higher oil prices and greater production.

Despite flat profitability, New Zealand companies in general have maintained low debt levels, to the point where some may consider capital repayments along the same lines as DB Group Ltd, Guy Hallwright at First NZ Capital said.
"There are a number of companies that now have pretty low debt levels and I think it's odds on that some of them will do similar things (to DB)," Hallwright said.

"We are on a cyclical low point, but I think that by the second half of the year things will be looking a bit different," he said, adding the lagged effect of last December's easing would take time to flow through, possibly in the second half.
But Cavill White's Turkington was not so sure.
"The thing that has changed is that we are now much more pessimistic about the chances for an upturn in late 1997, early 1998," he said.

While it was possible the economy would benefit from increased government spending over the current fiscal year and beyond, it was equally likely that such benefits would be counteracted by the compensating impact of monetary conditions, he said. -- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
